Chapter 10: Moving Toward Justice and Collective Liberation
You know, healing the body is incredibly personal, but it’s also deeply political. If we really want healing to take root, we can’t just look inward—we’ve got to challenge the systems that create and reinforce racialized trauma in the first place. It means moving past just changing ourselves, and stepping into collective action.
Imagine a group of friends. They’re tired of watching the same injustices play out in their city, year after year. So, they decide to do something. They show up at city council meetings, they organize community forums, and they start working with local leaders to push for real change.
Was it easy? Not at all. It was slow, sometimes downright frustrating. There were days when it felt like nothing was moving. But, little by little, they saw small victories—a new policy here, a safer park there. And what stood out was that it wasn’t just about changing laws. It was about transforming the way people think and feel. Changing hearts and minds.
Here’s something you might not have considered: doing justice work is actually a way of healing. When people come together to demand fairness, your body feels it. There’s this sense of agency—of hope, and of possibility. Even your nervous system, which might’ve gotten used to bracing for disappointment, starts to learn that real change can happen.
Of course, this work is never really finished. There will always be setbacks, moments when you feel like giving up, and resistance from those who are invested in keeping things just as they are. But the key is to keep moving—to lean on your support system, and to celebrate every single step forward, no matter how small.
What becomes clear is this: healing and justice go hand in hand. You simply can’t have one without the other. As we heal—both as individuals and as communities—we unlock the ability to imagine and build a world where everyone, yes everyone, has the chance to truly thrive.
